body.text: Charging infrastructure lagging in WA's Pilbara despite Australia's EV sales surge
In short:
Electric vehicle drivers say Western Australia's charging network is failing to keep up with demand in the state's Pilbara.
The state government is being called on to provide more support for remote charging infrastructure.
What's next?
An EV expert says a big picture approach is needed to ensure freight electrification is considered for future chargers.
Travellers say Western Australia's high-profile "electric highway" is failing to keep pace with demand, and risks deterring road trips to remote parts of the state.

Launched in 2025 to significant fanfare, WA's electric vehicle charging network comprises 110 charging points between Mundrabilla, on the Nullarbor Plain in the state's remote south-east, through to Kununurra in the East Kimberley.
But the network has been plagued by reports of broken chargers and malfunctioning equipment, triggering increased "range anxiety" from drivers navigating remote parts of the state.

With EVs outselling petrol and diesel cars in Australia for the first time in August, Australia's North West tourism chief executive officer Bill Tatchell said EV infrastructure was becoming more crucial.
"The distances here are enormous, so confidence in the availability and reliability of charging is probably even more important in the North West than it is in metropolitan areas," he said.
"The state's EV Network has made a significant difference by creating a charging spine through the region, but over time we will need to keep building on that."
Perth woman Catherin Robinson is a new EV owner who undertook a 1,500 kilometre drive north to Karratha to visit family, after owning her car for only two weeks.
Ms Robinson described her journey as "sink or swim".
"Range anxiety was very, very real,"
she said.
"There needs to be more availability, closer together, not so sparse, and chargers that work."
Ms Robinson believed the lack of chargers meant travellers could not properly explore the region.
"We had to go from A to B and even though we wanted to … it wasn't worth the time charging to go off," she said.
"It could never have been a spur-of-the-moment decision to go and explore a bit more."
Bill Tatchell said improvements and access to the region's chargers would be critical as EV use grew.
"Road trips are fundamental to tourism in the North West," he said.
"As more Australians move into electric vehicles we need to make sure owning an EV doesn't become a reason not to travel north."
Wary heading to the country
Michael Kerr, another EV owner from Perth, made the 2,700km round trip to Karijini National Park this year and said he would be unlikely to make the trip again.
Mr Kerr said he had to plan the multi-day journey around broken chargers and waiting hours to power up at slow chargers added to the stress of the trip.
"You have to keep an eye on what's working," he said.
"You have to be careful about judging the distances you travel between charges."
At one stop, Mr Kerr barely made it to the charger, rolling in with only 20km of range left on the EV's battery.
Having travelled to Karijini on previous trips in a petrol vehicle, Mr Kerr described the charging network as "pathetic" and has written to the state government about his concerns.
"It's an EV charging line … once you get off the main [North West Coastal] highway, it's bad, really bad," he said.
"We won't be doing that trip again anytime soon, now we're pretty wary about heading off to the country."
Fail grade for network
In its 2026 State of the EVs Report released last month, the Electric Vehicle Council rated the WA government three out of 10 across 26 metrics.
The report found the WA government was underperforming, despite its strong financial position, with weak supports for charging infrastructure and passenger and freight vehicles.
Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the state government had provided the backbone of EV charging infrastructure.
But she did not respond when asked whether the government would consider expanding the network.
"We've connected more than 7,000 kilometres of Western Australia across 110 charging points," Ms Sanderson said.
"We've also supported WA organisations and businesses to install chargers at destinations across the state through three rounds of Charge Up grants."
'Tombstones in car parks'
EV expert Kai Li Lim said there was often a "bigger and better" mentality when it came to chargers, but slower, cheaper options in strategic locations could be more affordable.
"If you're going to stay at national parks, for example, and you may be parking your car for two to four hours at a time, you don't need to have the big fat DC chargers charging your car," he said.
Dr Lim said maintenance must be factored in when new chargers were commissioned, whether publicly or privately owned.
"We are starting to see this whole notion of chargers … almost like tombstones in the car parks,"
he said.
"Nobody wants to take ownership of the chargers anymore.
"A charger breaks down in the Pilbara and you have technicians over east, when do we send the technician over to the Pilbara to fix the chargers?"
Dr Lim said there was also a bigger industrial decarbonisation picture to consider when weighing up the value of remote charging networks.
"It's important to make sure that the infrastructure that we build across the country, and not just in WA, is also supporting freight electrification."
